What makes the crab so amazing?

Walking sideways, the crab is a beloved beach friend with a hard shell and big claws. There's a fun reason behind that sideways walk.

This book brings together all sorts of stories about the crab, including crab facts, the crab's sideways walk, and crab molting.

content.text:
Nature and science facts about the crab

A crab's body is covered by a hard shell (exoskeleton) like a suit of armor. Because of the way its leg joints are built, walking sideways is faster and easier than walking forward, so it moves sideways. Its big claws are used for all kinds of things — grabbing food, defending itself, and sending signals. As it grows, it sheds the shell that has become too small and puts on a new one — this is called molting, and right after shedding its body is soft, so it stays hidden.

Parent guide — how to spark curiosity

Try playing a game where you walk sideways like a crab. Tell your child "when the shell gets too small, it sheds it and changes into a new one (molting)," and finding crab holes in a tidal flat makes it even more exciting.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q. Why does a crab walk sideways?
A. Because of the way its leg joints are built, walking sideways is faster and easier than walking forward.

Q. How does a crab grow?
A. It "molts" — shedding the shell that has become too small and changing into a new one. Right after shedding, its body is soft.

Q. How can we observe it at home?
A. It's great to play the sideways-walk game and to find crab holes in a tidal flat.
